The Iran blockade started March 21 and oil prices spiked, so gasoline and heating costs are about to hit your next grocery receipt and rent bill within weeks.
The Fed's 2% target is now a full percentage point away from core inflation, which means rate cuts are off the table and borrowing stays expensive through mid-2026.
moderate: Core PCE at 3.0% YoY in February, up from expectations, reflects a combination of energy pass-through (WTI above $100 briefly) and sticky services inflation that the Fed cannot ignore.
Historically, energy shocks at this magnitude take 6 to 8 weeks to fully propagate through the CPI basket, so April and May readings will likely show headline CPI climbing toward 3.5% or higher.
The 130 basis point gap between core PCE (3.0%) and the Fed's target (2%) means officials have zero flexibility to cut rates, contradicting market pricing for 2 to 3 cuts by year-end.
expert: Core PCE 3.0% YoY in February with a 50 basis point upside surprise indicates momentum; crude at $97.87 and the Strait of Hormuz blockade (March 21) guarantee additional prints above 3.2% through Q2.

Services inflation (the sticky component) has historically proven slow to reverse when energy-driven, and the 3.25% policy rate sits only 25 basis points above core PCE, leaving no buffer for central bank credibility if headline CPI exceeds 3.8%.

Forward guidance now hinges on whether energy prices revert (unlikely before May 2026) or stabilize; if WTI stays above $90, terminal core PCE settles at 3.1% to 3.3%, forcing the Fed to hold rates at 3.25% through Q3 2026.

beginner: Unemployment at 4.2% sounds normal, but combined with energy shocks and slowing growth (0.5% in Q4 2025), jobless claims are about to start rising.
Energy price spikes typically cut hiring within one to two months, so companies will pause new jobs in May and June even if they have not announced layoffs yet.
If unemployment drifts above 4.5% by summer, the Fed will finally have an excuse to cut rates, but that only happens if the economy really weakens.
moderate: The 4.2% unemployment rate remains below the Fed's estimated neutral rate of 4.5%, but Q4 2025 growth of 0.5% annualized means the labor market is already softening beneath the surface.
Energy cost shocks historically precede a 40 to 60 basis point rise in the unemployment rate within 2 to 3 quarters, mirroring the 2011 and 2022 experiences.
Watch for initial jobless claims to cross 250,000 per week (currently around 215,000) by late May; that signals the Strait of Hormuz disruption is translating into actual layoff announcements.
expert: The 4.2% unemployment rate with negative real wage growth (nominal wage gains below 3.0% core PCE) indicates labor market resilience is hollow; any decline in hours worked will push the U3 rate above 4.5% by Q3 2026.

Historically, a 30 to 50 basis point energy shock yield curve steepening (currently at +70bps) correlates with a 75 basis point rise in unemployment within 18 months; current trajectory points to 5.0%+ by Q4 2026.

Forward implication: unemployment crossing 4.5% is the Fed's off-ramp for rate cuts, but only if core PCE remains sticky above 2.8%; if both conditions trigger simultaneously by July, expect 50 basis points of cuts by year-end.

beginner: The budget deficit sits at 6.9% of GDP, which means the government is borrowing nearly $7 for every $100 of economic output, and that number will get worse before it gets better.
Slower economic growth (0.5% in Q4 2025) means less tax revenue, so the deficit will expand toward 7.5% of GDP by mid-2026 unless Congress cuts spending or raises taxes.
Rising interest rates on government debt mean more tax dollars go to paying bond holders instead of schools, roads, or defense, which is why this deficit matters beyond the headline number.
moderate: At 6.9% of GDP, the deficit is running near 2020 crisis levels even though the economy is not in a recession, reflecting structural spending above revenue without a cyclical excuse.

Slower growth combined with the 10Y bond yield at 4.31% (up 80 basis points from end-2025) means deficit financing costs rise at the exact moment tax receipts are falling due to energy shocks and demand softness.

Historically, deficits above 6.5% of GDP during low-unemployment periods (4.2% jobless rate) force either fiscal consolidation or persistent higher real interest rates; the current setup suggests the latter, crowding out private investment.
expert: The 6.9% deficit with 10Y yields at 4.31% and GDP growth decelerating to 0.5% annualized (Q4 2025) creates an unsustainable fiscal trajectory; debt-to-GDP projections now exceed 130% by 2027 without policy adjustment.

Interest payments on federal debt will consume 3.1% of GDP by 2027 (up from 1.8% in 2019), crowding mandatory spending and capping discretionary room; every 50 basis point yield rise adds $80 billion to annual costs.

Forward signal: if unemployment hits 4.5%+ by Q3 2026, automatic stabilizers (UI payouts, reduced income tax receipts) will push the deficit above 8% of GDP unless the administration imposes spending cuts or revenue measures, triggering a fiscal consolidation shock.

beginner: The current account deficit of 3.7% of GDP means America imports far more than it exports, and rising energy prices from the Iran blockade will make that worse.
When oil prices spike, American consumers and businesses pay more to foreign sellers, which widens the trade deficit and means more U.S. dollars flowing overseas.
A bigger current account deficit can eventually weaken the dollar, making imports even more expensive for Americans, so watch the USD/DXY closely over the next two months.
moderate: The 3.7% current account deficit reflects both a structural trade deficit (goods imports exceed exports by $800+ billion annually) and income flows; crude at $97.87 guarantees the deficit widens toward 4.2% of GDP by Q2 2026.
Historically, energy shocks of this magnitude (WTI above $100 for weeks) add 30 to 50 basis points to the current account deficit within one quarter as the energy import bill surges.

The deficit is partially offset by capital inflows (foreign buyers of U.S. Treasury bonds and equities), but those flows depend on yield differentials; if foreign yields rise faster than 4.31%, the financing dynamic breaks and the dollar weakens.
expert: The 3.7% current account deficit combined with the Strait of Hormuz blockade (March 21 onset) and crude at $97.87 will push the energy trade deficit alone toward $45 billion per month by May 2026, expanding the current account gap to 4.0%+ of GDP.

Net income flows (investment returns to foreigners) currently offset 0.8 percentage points of the current account shortfall, but if 10Y yields peak and then decline (likely by Q3 2026), foreigners repatriate capital and the current account deteriorates to 4.5%+ of GDP.

Forward implication: a current account deficit above 4% of GDP in a low-growth environment (2.2% headline, 0.5% trailing) historically precedes a 5% to 8% dollar depreciation within 12 months; USD/DXY at 98.4 is vulnerable to a drop toward 93 to 95 if growth disappoints again.

beginner: The Fed's interest rate sits at 3.25%, which is high enough to make mortgages and car loans expensive, and the central bank has no plans to cut it soon.
Core inflation is still at 3.0% YoY (in February), so even though the Fed paused rate hikes, officials will not lower rates until they see proof that prices are really coming down.
Borrowing money in April 2026 costs roughly the same as it did in early 2025, which means consumers and businesses are still feeling squeezed by higher costs.
moderate: The 3.25% policy rate remains 75 basis points above the Fed's likely neutral rate (around 2.5%), but core PCE at 3.0% means officials have zero room to cut until inflation moves meaningfully toward 2.5%.

Market pricing for 2 to 3 rate cuts by year-end ignores the sticky nature of services inflation and the fresh energy shock from the March 21 Strait blockade; the Fed's own guidance points to rates staying flat through Q2 2026.

If unemployment drifts above 4.5% without core inflation falling below 2.8%, the Fed faces a genuine policy dilemma (stagflation), and the next move would likely be a pause (no cuts, no hikes) rather than easing.
expert: The 3.25% policy rate with core PCE at 3.0% YoY (February, up from expectations) and the Strait blockade creating fresh energy shocks means the Fed's terminal rate for this cycle sits at 3.0% to 3.5%, not the 2.5% to 2.75% markets were pricing 60 days ago.

The 70 basis point yield curve steepening (10Y at 4.31%, fed funds at 3.25%) signals markets expect either a prolonged pause followed by late-cycle cuts (if growth falters to <1%) or a 50 basis point cut cycle beginning in Q4 2026.

Key forward watch: if core PCE remains above 2.8% in April and May while GDP growth disappoints (Q1 2026 annualized below 1.0%), the Fed will hold rates at 3.25% through September 2026, pushing the next cuts to late Q3, not summer.

beginner: The stock market is up just 0.4% year-to-date, which is essentially flat, meaning investors have made almost no money despite four months of trading.

Energy stocks are rallying because oil is expensive (WTI at $97.87), but most other companies are struggling because they have to pay more for fuel and pass those costs to consumers, which hurts profits.
If the economy slows further (Q4 2025 was only 0.5% growth) and unemployment starts rising, stocks could easily fall 5% to 10% from here, wiping out any year-to-date gains.
moderate: The 0.4% YTD gain masks severe sector divergence: energy and utilities are up 8% to 12% on oil strength, but tech, discretionary, and industrials are flat to down 3% as earnings expectations decline due to slower growth and higher financing costs.

Historically, equity markets deliver positive returns only when corporate earnings growth exceeds 5% YoY; current consensus expects 6% to 8% growth for 2026, but the Q4 2025 GDP revision (0.5%) and the March energy shock are forcing analyst downgrades.

The 10Y yield at 4.31% makes bonds competitive with stocks on a risk-adjusted basis for the first time since 2019, so expect equity valuations to compress another 5% to 8% if rates stay at 3.25% through Q3.
expert: The +0.4% YTD return with a 30% concentration in energy and utilities (rallying 10%+) while the broader market ex-energy is down 2% signals a complete lack of breadth; earnings revisions for 2026 are now declining at a 12% quarterly pace, the fastest since Q4 2022.

The S&P 500 P/E multiple is currently 19.5x 2026 estimated earnings; if consensus EPS drops 3% to 5% due to growth disappointment (likely by May 2026 earnings), valuations compress to 18.5x, implying a 5% to 8% downside to the index.

Forward signal: equity markets are pricing in a Fed rate cut cycle by Q4 2026, but if core PCE stays above 2.8% and unemployment remains below 4.5%, the Fed pauses instead, breaking the narrative that drove the small YTD rally; a reset lower toward SPX 5,200 to 5,300 (8% to 10% below current levels) becomes the base case.

beginner: The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.31%, which is the interest rate the government pays to borrow money for a decade, and it affects mortgage rates, car loans, and corporate borrowing costs.
Yields are high because inflation is still a problem (core PCE at 3.0%) and the Fed is not cutting rates, so bond investors demand more money to lend for long periods.
If energy prices fall over the next two months and inflation starts dropping, yields could come down toward 4.0%, which would help home buyers and businesses borrow more cheaply.
moderate: The 4.31% 10Y yield sits 106 basis points above the 3.25% policy rate, which is the steepest curve in three years and reflects market expectations for either eventual Fed cuts or persistent higher-for-longer rates.

Historically, 10Y yields move to 5%+ only during peak inflation scares or aggressive Fed tightening cycles; the current 4.31% suggests markets have priced in the Iran blockade shock but not a deeper stagflation outcome.

Watch for yield compression to 4.0% if Q1 2026 growth comes in below 1.0%, which would signal a bet that the Fed cuts 100 basis points by year-end; conversely, yields spike above 4.5% if core PCE stays above 3.0% in April.
expert: The 10Y yield at 4.31% with core PCE at 3.0% YoY implies a +131 basis point real yield, the highest since 2009; this pricing assumes either Fed cuts arrive in H2 2026 (requiring a 0.5% GDP growth print in Q1 2026) or inflation accelerates above 3.5% (unlikely without crude spiking above $120).

The 70 basis point curve steepening (2Y at 3.61%, 10Y at 4.31%) signals a 60% market probability of cuts beginning in September 2026, a 25% probability of a hard landing (recession, 150+ basis points of cuts by Q1 2027), and a 15% probability of held rates through 2026.

Forward implication: if the March 21 Iran blockade persists and WTI holds above $95 through May, the 10Y stays above 4.25%; if geopolitical tensions ease and crude falls to $80 to $85 by June, watch for a rapid 50 basis point drop in 10Y yields as markets reprice the entire Fed cut cycle forward to August 2026.

beginner: The yield curve is now positive at +70 basis points, meaning long-term bonds pay more interest than short-term bonds, which is the normal healthy situation.

For the past two years, the yield curve was inverted (short rates higher than long rates), which warned that a recession was coming; now that it has normalized, it suggests the recession might not be as bad as feared.
Keep watching this number: if the yield curve inverts again, it is a red flag that the economy is about to enter a downturn within 6 to 12 months.
moderate: The +70 basis point steepening from an inverted curve position two quarters ago indicates markets now expect the Fed to cut rates by late 2026, reversing the "higher for longer" expectations that dominated late 2025.

Historically, yield curve re-steepening after an inversion occurs 2 to 4 quarters before rate cuts actually begin; the current +70bps steepness suggests markets are positioning for cuts around September 2026.

However, the steepening is driven partly by long-term inflation expectations (10Y at 4.31%) rather than near-term Fed easing; if inflation data disappoints again in May (core PCE above 3.1%), the curve could flatten back toward +40bps, signaling delayed cuts.
expert: The +70 basis point curve (2Y at 3.61%, 10Y at 4.31%) has steepened 110 basis points since the December 2024 inversion, but the composition matters: 60bps of steepening is from 10Y yields rising, not 2Y yields falling, indicating the market is pricing inflation stickiness, not near-term Fed cuts.

Historically, curves remain steep (+50 to +100bps) only when nominal GDP growth (real growth + inflation) is expected to exceed 4% in outer years; current market pricing for 2027 implies a 3.5% to 4.0% nominal GDP, consistent with either 2% real growth + 1.5% to 2% inflation (soft landing) or 0.5% real growth + 3.5% inflation (stagflation).

Forward implication: if Q1 2026 GDP comes in below 1.0% annualized and unemployment is heading above 4.5%, watch for a 30 basis point flattening (curve to +40bps) by June 2026, signaling market repricing of a 75 to 100 basis point cut cycle; conversely, if core PCE stays above 3.0% through May, the curve stays steep or steepens further toward +100bps, delaying cuts until Q4 2026.

beginner: The dollar index (USD/DXY) is at 98.4, which measures the dollar's strength against a basket of other major currencies, and it is up sharply from a year ago.
A strong dollar makes American exports more expensive for foreign buyers, which hurts companies that sell overseas, but it makes imports cheaper for U.S. consumers.

If energy prices keep pushing inflation higher and the Fed stays stubborn about not cutting rates, the dollar could stay strong, which would make it harder for companies like Boeing and farmers to compete globally.
moderate: The USD/DXY at 98.4 is driven by higher U.S. real yields (10Y minus inflation expectations at +130bps) and the expectation that the Fed will hold rates higher for longer than other central banks.

Historically, the dollar strengthens when U.S. real yields exceed other developed markets by more than 100bps; that premium is now at 120 to 140bps against EUR, GBP, and JPY, which props up DXY at elevated levels.

Watch whether the Fed's rate hold through Q2 2026 and sticky inflation (core PCE above 2.8%) keep real yields elevated; if core PCE falls below 2.5% by July, real yields compress and DXY weakens toward 96 to 97.
expert: USD/DXY at 98.4 is sustained by a +130bps real 10Y yield (4.31% nominal minus 2% inflation expectations), the widest U.S. real yield advantage over the euro and pound since early 2023; this premium is partially artificial, driven by lingering Fed hawkishness priced into the curve.

The correlation between 10Y real yields and DXY is 0.82 historically; if 10Y yields fall from 4.31% to 4.0% (a base case if Q1 2026 GDP disappoints), DXY falls to 95.5 to 96.5 (a 2% to 3% depreciation), which adds 50 to 80bps to imported inflation.

Forward watch: the Strait of Hormuz blockade (March 21) supports the dollar short-term (safe-haven bid, energy revenues flow to dollar reserves), but if geopolitical risk eases and the Fed cuts in Q4 2026, DXY re-rates toward 92 to 94, a 5% to 6% depreciation from current levels that would be disinflationary for non-energy imports but inflationary for commodities (oil, metals, agriculture).

beginner: Measured in U.S. dollars, the stock market is down 3.12% year-to-date, which means if you invested in a broad stock index four months ago, you would have lost money even though the nominal index is up 0.4%.

The difference between these two numbers (0.4% up in index terms, 3.12% down in dollar terms) is confusing, but the simple version is this: stocks that are priced in foreign currencies lost extra value because the dollar strengthened.
If the dollar weakens over the next two months, the same stocks could recover their losses in dollar terms, even if the index itself stays flat.
moderate: The -3.12% YTD return in USD terms versus +0.4% in index terms reflects a 3.5% currency headwind from dollar strength (USD/DXY at 98.4, up 4% YTD); this means non-U.S. equity exposure lost an extra 3% to 4% for American investors in dollar terms.

Historically, strong dollar periods (DXY above 98) last 12 to 18 months before reversing; if the Fed cuts rates in Q4 2026 and the dollar weakens to 95 to 96, foreign stock exposure re-rates higher in dollar terms, creating a currency-driven gain of 3% to 4%.

For a U.S. investor, the -3.12% YTD loss is worse than headline earnings would suggest because international holdings (roughly 25% to 30% of broad indices) were dragged down by the dollar's 4% year-to-date rally.
expert: The -3.12% YTD return in USD versus +0.4% in index terms reveals a 350 basis point currency drag, with USD/DXY strength accounting for 75% of the underperformance; MSCI World ex-USA is down 2.5% in local currency terms but down 5.8% in dollar terms, amplifying the realized loss for U.S. dollar-based investors.

The currency headwind is structural if 10Y real yields stay at +130bps; however, if Fed rate cuts begin in Q4 2026 and 10Y yields fall to 3.8% to 4.0%, real yield compression of 30 to 50bps will drive DXY to 95 to 96, creating a 2% to 3% currency tailwind that could offset a flat to slightly negative equity return in local terms.

Forward implication: USD-denominated equity returns in 2026 are now a two-way bet between earnings (consensus +6% to 8%) and currency (DXY trajectory hinges on Fed cut timing); if the Fed delays cuts to Q4 2026 and DXY stays above 97, full-year 2026 USD stock returns compress to +2% to 4% despite positive earnings growth, whereas early cuts (August 2026) and DXY weakness to 95 could deliver +8% to 10% USD returns despite flat local equity markets.

beginner: Core inflation stuck at 3.0% in February, refusing to budge down despite the Fed's rate hikes. That's still a full point above target, so the Fed can't declare victory yet.

Oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz in March, forcing energy costs higher just when inflation looked sticky. Energy shocks have a nasty habit of spreading through the whole economy.
Growth collapsed to just 0.5% annualized in Q4 2025. When you mix weak growth with stubborn inflation, you get stagflation, and that's exactly what keeps policymakers up at night.
moderate: Core PCE at 3.0% in February signals the disinflationary trend stalled. The Fed cut rates to 3.64% expecting inflation to keep falling, but instead it's holding firm, forcing a rethink on how many more cuts make sense this year.

The Iran blockade pushed WTI crude to $97.87, replicating the supply shock playbook from 2022. Unlike that episode, unemployment sits at 4.4% and the Fed has already loosened policy, so stagflation risk looks real if energy prices stay elevated.

Q4 GDP at 0.5% annualized against a 2.2% full-year forecast tells you growth momentum evaporated entering 2026. A consumer squeeze is likely if wage gains can't outpace sticky inflation, pressuring the Fed to cut faster than the energy shock justifies.
expert: Core PCE 3.0% YoY in February with nominal wage growth running near 3.9% means real wage deceleration has reversed, removing the disinflationary tailwind the Fed counted on. The energy spike (Brent at $100, WTI at $97.87) reintroduced a supply-side inflation vector just as the Fed shifted to easing.

GDP annualized at 0.5% in Q4 2025 while core PCE sits 100bps above the 2% target creates the stagflation bind. The Fed faces a policy trilemma: cut to support activity, hold to fight inflation, or navigate a recession if supply shocks persist and demand collapses.

Watch whether the jobless rate (4.4%) holds or ticks up through Q2 2026. A labor market deterioration would vindicate rate cuts and argue for a faster cutting cycle, but only if energy prices roll over. If crude stays above $90 and unemployment rises together, the Fed has no good options.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The US dollar floats freely - its value is set by supply and demand in global markets. As the world's reserve currency, the dollar is the benchmark against which most other currencies are measured. The DXY index shown here is not a single exchange rate - it measures the dollar's strength against a basket of 6 major currencies (euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, Swiss franc). A DXY of 104 means the dollar is 4% stronger than the basket's baseline value of 100.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float. The dollar's value is market-determined with no intervention target. The Fed does not have an exchange rate mandate, though dollar strength has indirect policy implications via financial conditions and import prices. The DXY index measures USD against a basket of 6 major currencies.
fxRegime.expert: Pure free float with no FX intervention since the Plaza/Louvre era. The dollar operates as the global numeraire and primary reserve/invoicing currency (~58% of allocated reserves per IMF COFER). Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund exists but is dormant. Dollar valuation is a function of relative growth differentials, rate spreads, and safe-haven flows - the "dollar smile" framework applies.

GDP Growth.beginner: The US economy grew solidly in 2025 fuelled by consumer spending and a strong stock market, but growth is expected to slow in 2026 as tariffs raise costs and hiring weakens.
GDP Growth.moderate: US GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% for 2026 (above consensus), driven by OBBBA tax cuts and easier financial conditions, but tariff drag and a deteriorating labour market (unemployment trending toward 4.4%) pose meaningful downside risk.
GDP Growth.expert: Goldman forecasts US real GDP at 2.6% for 2026, outperforming consensus by 0.6pp on the strength of the OBBBA fiscal impulse and reduced tariff drag post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling; the Iran oil shock introduces a stagflationary supply-side headwind that could compress the growth rate by 0.3-0.5pp if Brent stays above $90 through Q2.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: US prices rose 2.4% in January compared to a year earlier, still above the Fed's 2% target, and the jump in oil prices from the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher again in the coming months.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: US CPI was 2.4% in January (ex-shutdown distortions ~2.7%), with tariff passthrough expected to add 0.3pp in H1 2026; the Iran energy shock could add a further 0.5-1.0pp, raising the risk that CPI reaches 3%+ by mid-year, complicating Fed rate-cut planning significantly.
Inflation (CPI).expert: US PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) ran at approximately 2.6% entering 2026; tariff-driven goods CPI uplift (+1.3-1.4% on imported durables in 2025) is now being compounded by an energy-driven CPI spike, and Goldman estimates the Iran shock alone could add 0.5pp to US CPI within 6 weeks if crude stays at current levels, a scenario the FOMC did not price in its December dot plot.

Unemployment.beginner: About 130,000 new jobs were created in January, fewer than expected, and the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4%, a sign the job market is cooling as businesses become more cautious about hiring.
Unemployment.moderate: January payrolls of 130,000 (private +172k, federal -42k) masked underlying weakness: ex-healthcare, private sector job creation was just 6,500; the unemployment rate has drifted to 4.4%, and IT employment fell 12,000, consistent with AI-driven displacement beginning to register in headline data.
Unemployment.expert: The K-shaped US labour market (healthcare/social assistance absorbing +123,500 jobs while IT shed 12,000 and manufacturing and wholesale contracted) is consistent with AI-driven productivity reallocation depressing labour demand in white-collar sectors; the FOMC's dual-mandate tension is now acute as unemployment trends higher even as tariff-and-energy-driven inflation runs above target.

Budget Deficit.beginner: The US government is borrowing heavily, with a deficit of around 6% of GDP, meaning the government spends much more than it collects in taxes, and tariff revenues of about $194 billion in 2025 only partially offset the gap.
Budget Deficit.moderate: The US fiscal deficit is running near 6% of GDP, sustained by structural entitlement spending and the OBBBA tax cut impulse; tariff revenues ($194bn above 2022-24 average in 2025) partially offset cost, but the Section 122 tariff (replacing struck-down IEEPA tariffs) adds only ~$22.3bn annually, leaving a structurally wide deficit.
Budget Deficit.expert: Post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling (Feb 20), the US tariff revenue base shifted to Section 232 + Section 122 (temporary 10%) + pre-existing Section 301 China tariffs; TPC estimates total tariff revenue of $194bn in 2026, but the OBBBA's multi-trillion dollar cost and rising debt service (10-year Treasury ~4.2%) are widening the structural primary deficit, constraining the Fed's ability to QE in a crisis without fiscal dominance concerns.

Current Account.beginner: The US buys far more from the rest of the world than it sells, creating a large trade deficit that tariffs were supposed to reduce, but the deficit has not meaningfully narrowed despite record tariff revenues.
Current Account.moderate: The US current account deficit has remained stubbornly wide despite tariff-driven import compression; the Tax Foundation estimates tariffs have 'not meaningfully altered the trade deficit' as dollar strength offsets competitiveness gains; the Iran oil shock could temporarily widen the energy trade deficit before domestic production responds.
Current Account.expert: The persistence of the US current account deficit despite historically high tariff rates confirms the Lerner symmetry theorem in practice: tariffs on imports are offset by equivalent tariffs on exports via currency adjustment and income effects; the structural determinant is the gap between domestic saving and investment, a gap that OBBBA fiscal expansion is actively widening by reducing national saving.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Federal Reserve has kept interest rates at 4.25-4.5%, pausing its rate cuts from last year, as it waits to see whether prices keep falling toward its 2% target, which is now more uncertain because of the oil price spike.
Policy Rate.moderate: The FOMC has been on hold at 4.25-4.5% since late 2025; markets that had priced June cuts before the Iran shock have now pushed the first cut expectation to July-September; FOMC members face a classic stagflation dilemma and NY Fed's Williams has explicitly said tariff-driven inflation has 'temporarily stalled' progress toward the 2% target.
Policy Rate.expert: The FOMC's reaction function is now constrained on multiple dimensions: the dual tariff-and-energy supply shock argues against rate cuts (inflation upside risk), while a cooling labour market and deteriorating business confidence argue for easing; the December dot plot (two cuts in 2026) is now likely inoperative, and any shift toward the 'stagflation hold' scenario would materially re-price the front end of the US rates curve with knock-on effects on EM capital flows and USD strength.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, which is slow enough to make people worry about job security and wage growth.
The rebound in Q3 2025 came from the Bank of Canada cutting interest rates, but that sugar rush won't last if exports keep falling.
Tariff uncertainty from the Trump administration's USMCA renegotiation means businesses are holding back on hiring and investment until they know what's coming.
moderate: At 1.7% growth, Canada trails most G7 peers (US is running 2.5%+), and the Q2 contraction shows the economy lost steam before the recent bounce.
The Q3 rebound relied heavily on rate cuts and stimulus, not on underlying demand strength, which means growth could stall again once policy support fades.
USMCA renegotiation talks extending tariffs to Chinese goods flowing through Mexico and Canada inject enough doubt that firms are delaying capex, adding a structural headwind to expansion.
expert: 1.7% annualized growth masks quarterly volatility (Q2 contracted, Q3 rebounded), and forward guidance from the BoC signals only modest acceleration unless trade tensions ease.
The growth impulse from 275bps of cumulative rate cuts (from 5% to 2.25%) is already priced in; next upside depends on USMCA clarity and a stabilization in goods exports.
Watch for Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 data: if growth slips below 1.5% annualized or unemployment rises above 6.7%, the BoC may resume cuts despite inflation at target, signaling stagflation risk.

beginner: Inflation at 2% means the Bank of Canada has nailed its target, so prices are stable and your paycheck buys what it should.
The BoC cut rates aggressively because inflation had come down so far and so fast, not because demand was roaring.
Watch wage growth: if paychecks stay flat while inflation stays at 2%, workers lose purchasing power in real terms.
moderate: At 2%, Canadian CPI sits right at the BoC's midpoint target, a sharp reversal from 2022-23 highs above 8%, and gives the central bank room to prioritize growth over price stability.
The disinflationary grind accelerated in 2024-25 partly because energy prices cooled and the loonie weakened (imports got cheaper), but tariff risks could reverse that if trade barriers spike.

Core inflation measures (trimmed mean, weighted median) likely sit 50-75bps above headline, suggesting some underlying stickiness in services; wage acceleration would threaten the BoC's comfort at 2%.
expert: CPI at 2.0% with a yield curve at +111bps and real rates (policy rate minus inflation) at 0.25% suggests the BoC is priced for a soft landing, but tariff pass-through could push headline CPI to 2.5-3% within two quarters.
The BoC's 275bp easing cycle was front-loaded because slack opened faster than expected; further cuts hinge on whether core PCE equivalents stay anchored below 2.3% through 2026.

Monitor for second-round wage effects: if wage growth accelerates above 3% annualized while unemployment edges below 6%, the risk of re-acceleration to 2.5% CPI in H2 2026 rises sharply, forcing the BoC to pause or reverse cuts.

beginner: At 6.5%, Canada's jobless rate has drifted up from pre-pandemic lows, meaning fewer people are getting called back to work and the job market is softer than before.
Slack in the labor market gives the Bank of Canada permission to keep rates low, but it also means wage pressures are mild and workers have less bargaining power.
If unemployment keeps climbing toward 7%, companies will feel even more pressure to cut, and that feeds into slower spending.
moderate: Canada's 6.5% jobless rate is roughly 150bps above the pre-2020 trend, and Q2-Q3 weakness in export-heavy sectors (forestry, energy) pushed unemployment higher even as the BoC was cutting.

Participation rate dynamics matter: if the rise in joblessness reflects discouraged workers leaving the labor force rather than job losses, the real slack is smaller, and wage inflation risk is higher than the 6.5% headline suggests.
Unlike the US (where unemployment is 3.9%), Canada's softer labor market reflects trade exposure and less fiscal support, which explains why the BoC can cut aggressively without risking overheating.
expert: At 6.5% with labor force participation around 63.5%, the employment rate sits 130bps below pre-COVID trend, signaling a structural tightness (aging workforce, interprovincial migration) disguised by cyclical slack from trade shocks.

Unemployment duration and new jobless claims data are key: if average duration stays above 15 weeks and initial claims remain elevated through Q2 2026, the BoC may resume cuts even if headline unemployment edges higher, prioritizing growth risks.

Watch the sectoral breakdown: goods-producing unemployment (likely 7%+) vs. services (likely 6%); if goods sectors remain depressed through tariff cycles while services pick up, uneven recovery could muddy the BoC's rate path.

beginner: Canada's government is spending 1.5% more than it brings in each year, which means it's borrowing to cover the gap, and that money has to come from somewhere.
This deficit is small compared to what countries ran during COVID, but it's still larger than what Canada had before 2020, so the government has less room to borrow in a crisis.
If the deficit doesn't shrink, interest payments on all that debt will eat up more tax revenue, leaving less for schools, hospitals, and defense.
moderate: At 1.5% of GDP, Canada's budget deficit is modest by post-2008 standards (the US runs 6%+), but it's persistent, which means the debt-to-GDP ratio stays elevated even during a cyclical expansion.

The BoC's aggressive easing cycle (275bps of cuts since mid-2024) was premature given the deficit: the government was running loose fiscal while the central bank loosened monetary policy simultaneously, a policy mix that usually overheats demand.

Watch for fiscal drag in 2026-27: if revenue growth lags spending pressures (aging costs, defense commitments) and growth stays below 2%, the deficit could widen, forcing hard choices on spending or taxes.
expert: The 1.5% deficit in 2025 sits above the structural deficit (roughly 1%), implying cyclical slack is not yet large enough to justify continued loose fiscal; if growth rebounds to 2.5% by 2026, the deficit should fall toward 0.8-1.0%.

Debt service costs (roughly 3% of revenue) are manageable now, but a 100bp rise in real rates would push net interest payments to 3.5% of revenue within two years, crowding out discretionary spending and constraining the fiscal impulse.

Monitor the federal government's gross debt issuance: if deficits persist at 1.5% of GDP while growth stays below 2% and the yield curve normalizes (narrowing from +111bps), fiscal credibility could erode, pushing the CAD lower and real rates higher.

beginner: Canada is running a small trade deficit of 0.5% of GDP, meaning the country is buying more stuff from abroad than it's selling, and that gap is being filled by foreigners lending money.
This deficit is driven by weak exports (oil, metals, lumber are all down), which ties back to trade uncertainty and slower global demand.
If exports don't bounce back soon, Canada will need to attract more foreign investment to cover the gap, which means higher interest rates or a weaker currency.
moderate: At 0.5% of GDP, Canada's current account deficit is modest but structural: the country runs persistent deficits in goods trade (now worsening due to tariff uncertainty), offset partly by services and income flows.

The weakness in exports reflects two shocks: lower commodity prices (oil and metals) and USMCA renegotiation risks that are slowing US import demand; without a rebound in either, the deficit could widen to 1% of GDP by 2026.

Capital inflows (FDI and portfolio investment) still exceed the current account deficit, but a sharp slowdown in FDI due to trade uncertainty could force either a currency depreciation (CAD/USD to 0.70) or a rise in domestic interest rates to attract foreign capital.
expert: The 0.5% current account deficit masks a goods trade deficit of roughly 2% of GDP offset by a services surplus (TMT, finance) and net income flows; goods exports are down 8% YoY while imports fell only 3%, widening the goods gap to near-record levels.

With CAD/USD at 0.73 (roughly 5% weaker than early 2024), the currency depreciation should theoretically improve competitiveness, but export volumes remain depressed, suggesting demand factors dominate price elasticity.

Watch for capital flow reversal: if tariff uncertainty deepens and global risk appetite fades, foreign investors may reduce Canadian exposure, forcing either a current account rebalancing through sharper CAD depreciation (to 0.68-0.70) or a sharp rise in real rates (100-150bps higher) to maintain flows.

beginner: The Bank of Canada cut its key interest rate to 2.25%, down from 5% just a year ago, which makes borrowing cheaper for mortgages, car loans, and business loans.

The BoC cut so aggressively because inflation had come down and the economy was weakening, but the lag between rate cuts and their effect on the real economy means the cuts are only now starting to boost activity.
Watch to see if the BoC pauses or cuts again: if inflation pops back above 2.3% or unemployment drops sharply, expect them to stay put.
moderate: At 2.25%, the BoC has cut 275bps since June 2024 (when the rate was 5%), a pace unusually fast and driven by a sharp disinflationary cycle and cyclical growth weakness that surprised even the central bank.

The BoC signaled in its April 2026 guidance that it will proceed slowly with further cuts, implying the terminal rate for this easing cycle sits around 1.75-2%, meaning only 50bps of cuts remain if growth disappoints.

The policy rate now sits only 25bps above the inflation rate, leaving little room for error: if tariffs push inflation to 2.5-2.7% while growth stays below 1.5%, the BoC faces a dilemma of holding rates steady (risking recession) or cutting through 2% inflation (risking a re-acceleration).
expert: The 275bp easing cycle from 5% to 2.25% is the fastest pace since 1992-93 and reflects the BoC's view that r-star (the neutral rate) has fallen to 1.5-1.75%, implying current policy at 2.25% is slightly restrictive by the BoC's own framework.

Forward guidance markets are pricing in only 25bps of additional cuts through end-2026, with a terminal rate near 2%; this assumes no major trade shocks and gradual return to 2% growth; a tariff escalation or slower-than-expected demand recovery would trigger 75-100bps of additional cuts.

The key risk: if tariff-driven inflation pushes core PCE-equivalent measures above 2.3% (current estimate is 2.1%) while unemployment edges above 6.7%, the BoC will face pressure to pause cuts; if that coincides with US real rate strength (10Y yield at 3.29%), capital will flow south and CAD will weaken past 0.70, amplifying import inflation and forcing a tough policy choice.

beginner: Canada's stock market is up 6.3% so far in 2026, which is solid but it's trailing the US market and reflects investor caution about the economy.
The gains are mostly in big defensive stocks (banks, utilities) rather than growth, which tells you that investors are not betting on a strong recovery.
Watch for earnings reports: if companies keep missing on margins due to weak demand and tariffs, the market's gains could evaporate quickly.
moderate: At +6.3% YTD, the TSX is outperforming the S&P 500 when measured in CAD but massively underperforming in USD terms (+2.78%), because the loonie weakness (now 0.73) is a drag on US-denominated returns for foreign investors.

The gains are concentrated in financials and energy, sectors that benefit from lower rates and commodity price hope, while tech and discretionary lag; this split suggests the market is pricing in slower growth and modest inflation.

Valuation multiples on the TSX are roughly 15x 2026E earnings, in line with historical averages, implying limited upside unless growth surprises; with the BoC pausing cuts and tariff risk looming, the market is fairly priced, not cheap.
expert: The TSX's +6.3% YTD in CAD terms masks severe underperformance in USD (+2.78%), a 350bp gap driven entirely by CAD depreciation (0.73 vs. 0.77 at year-end 2025); for USD-based investors, the currency drag is the dominant driver, not equity fundamentals.

Equal-weight and small-cap indices are materially weaker than the cap-weighted TSX, indicating that large-cap cyclicals (energy, materials, financials) have rallied on multiple expansion, not earnings growth; if tariffs dampen global growth, multiple compression could erase 2-3 years of gains.

Watch the TSX futures curve (March 2027 vs. spot): if the market reprices tariff impact or Q4 2025 earnings disappoint, weakness could cascade to 14.5x multiples (15% downside), particularly if the BoC is forced to cut 75bps through 2026 (signaling growth-at-risk), while USD strength drives CAD below 0.71.

beginner: Canada's 10-year bond yield is at 3.29%, which is what you get paid if you lend money to the government for a decade, and it's lower than US yields because Canada's economy is weaker.
The yield dropped sharply over the past year because the Bank of Canada cut rates and investors got spooked about growth, so they bought bonds as a safe bet.
If the economy improves, yields will rise as investors demand higher returns; if recession fears grow, yields will fall further.
moderate: At 3.29%, Canada's 10Y yield sits roughly 40bps below the equivalent US Treasury (3.70%), a spread that reflects Canada's growth discount and the perception that the BoC has more room to cut than the Fed.

The 10Y yield has compressed sharply since Q2 2025 (when it was near 4%) as the market repriced the BoC's easing cycle and tariff risks dampened growth expectations, but it's still 50bps above the BoC's likely terminal policy rate (2.25%), suggesting term premium is pricing in structural risk.

Watch for flow dynamics: if US yields rise on stronger growth or inflation surprises, Canadian yields will follow, but the spread will likely widen to 50-60bps if the BoC cuts further while the Fed holds steady, creating hedging opportunities.
expert: The 10Y at 3.29% implies a forward rate path (2-10Y segment) of roughly 2.5%, consistent with the BoC pricing in 75bps of cumulative cuts through 2026 and stabilization near 2%; this forward curve has compressed 30bps since January as tariff uncertainty rose, signaling lower growth priced in.

Real yield on the 10Y (nominal yield minus inflation expectations) sits near 1.3%, elevated relative to pre-COVID norms (1.0%) due to term premium reflecting fiscal sustainability concerns and policy uncertainty; if tariffs accelerate, real yields could spike as inflation fears compete with growth fears.

Monitor US-Canada 10Y spread: if it widens past 60bps due to Fed hawkishness or if it narrows back to 30bps due to tariff-driven recession fears, the move will drive CAD volatility; a spike to 4%+ on US yields (coupled with Canada staying at 3.2%) would likely trigger a sub-0.71 CAD on capital flight.

beginner: Canada's yield curve is normal and upward sloping, meaning long-term interest rates are 111 basis points higher than short-term rates, which is healthy and tells you the market expects the economy to keep growing.
A normal curve is good news because an inverted curve (where short-term rates are higher) usually signals a recession is coming.
Watch if this spread narrows: if the 10-year yield falls faster than short-term rates rise, it could be a warning sign that investors are getting nervous about the future.
moderate: At +111bps, Canada's 2-10Y curve is steep compared to the US (roughly 80bps) and steeper than pre-COVID averages (80bps), reflecting both expectations for multiple BoC cuts through 2026 and a term premium that prices in uncertainty around tariffs and fiscal sustainability.

The curve steepness is unusual for an economy with slack (6.5% unemployment) and soft growth (1.7%), and it suggests markets are pricing in either a notable recovery in 2026-27 or a "lower for longer" scenario where short rates stay near 2%; both scenarios imply a significant revision to near-term growth expectations.

Watch for flattening: if the Fed holds rates steady while the BoC cuts another 75bps, Canada's 2-10Y could narrow to 80-90bps, bringing it closer to US steepness; a sharp narrowing to 60bps would signal recession fears are rising.
expert: The 2-10Y spread at +111bps is 30bps steeper than the 2-year forward curve (implied 2-10Y rate 2 years out), suggesting the market expects either a flattening from policy normalization or a notable re-steepening from a demand shock; the discrepancy implies uncertainty about the transmission mechanism and growth trajectory.

Decomposing the 111bps: roughly 75bps reflects the market's pricing of future rate cuts (BoC at 1.75-2.0% terminal, 2Y yields pricing in 75bps of cumulative easing), while 36bps reflects term and option premium; if tariff fears spike or recession odds shift from 15% to 30%, the premium collapses and the spread narrows to 75-80bps fast.

Scenario monitoring: if tariffs accelerate and consensus growth expectations for 2026 fall from 2.0% to 1.2%, expect 2Y yields to drop 40-50bps while 10Y yields hold near 3.2%, creating a 60-70bps spread; conversely, if tariff fears ease and growth reverts to 2.2%, 2Y yields rise 30bps while 10Y yields stay flat, widening the curve to 130-140bps.

beginner: The Canadian dollar is trading at 0.73 US dollars, which means it has gotten weaker over the past year and it makes imports more expensive for Canadians while making exports cheaper for foreigners.
A weaker loonie is good for exports and companies that sell abroad, but bad for consumers buying American products or planning a vacation south of the border.
The weakness reflects that Canada's growth is slower and weaker than the US, so investors are selling CAD and buying USD.
moderate: At 0.73, the CAD is near the lowest level since 2020 (when it briefly touched 0.68), a 7% depreciation since early 2024, driven by growth divergence (Canada 1.7% vs. US 2.5%+) and capital outflows as tariff uncertainty makes Canadian assets less attractive.

The currency weakness should be supporting export competitiveness, but export volumes remain depressed, suggesting the weakness reflects capital flight risk premium more than a positive valuation adjustment; if tariff fears ease, the CAD could rebound 2-3 cents quickly.

Watch relative interest rates: with the BoC cutting to 2.25% and the Fed holding at 5%, the 275bp rate differential is a historic headwind for CAD; if the Fed cuts while the BoC pauses, the differential narrows and CAD stabilizes, but only if growth fears recede.
expert: The CAD at 0.73 reflects a 7% depreciation from 0.79 in early 2024, with 4% of that move driven by interest rate differentials (BoC -275bp vs. Fed +0bp) and 3% from tariff risk premium and capital flight; the real effective exchange rate (CAD inflation-adjusted vs. trading partners) has depreciated 5%, modestly improving competitiveness.

Forward markets price CAD at 0.715 (3-month forward), implying a 50bp depreciation, consistent with market expectations that tariff fears will keep capital flows negative through Q2 2026; if USMCA negotiations conclude without major escalation, a snapback to 0.75-0.76 is possible within weeks.

Monitor flows: if non-resident purchases of Canadian equities and bonds fall below $2B CAD per month (currently running $2.5-3B), further depreciation past 0.71 is likely; conversely, if foreign direct investment rebounds (currently tracking $12B annually, down from $22B pre-2023), stabilization at 0.72-0.74 becomes more likely. Watch Fed-BoC rate expectations: every 25bp narrowing in the differential supports 0.50-0.75 cents of CAD appreciation.

beginner: Canada's stock market is up just 2.78% in US dollar terms in 2026, which is much weaker than it looks in Canadian dollars (6.3%) because the Canadian dollar got weaker.
For a US investor or anyone counting money in dollars, the currency damage wiped out most of the stock market gains.
This tells you that buying Canadian stocks was a bad bet this year because you lost money on the currency exchange, not because the stocks themselves didn't do well.
moderate: At +2.78% in USD terms, the TSX is severely underperforming the S&P 500 (up 12%+ YTD), with the 9pt gap driven entirely by CAD depreciation from 0.77 to 0.73 (a 5% currency drag), while the equity market itself gained roughly 6.3% in local currency.

This mismatch is unusual: normally, a weaker currency amplifies stock returns for foreigners in strong exporting economies, but Canada's exports are depressed despite CAD weakness, suggesting the currency move reflects risk-off sentiment more than fundamental competitiveness gains.

For global investors, Canadian equities face a double headwind: modest local currency gains (6.3%) combined with structural currency weakness (5% depreciation), making the asset class unattractive unless CAD stabilizes; wait for either growth stabilization or USMCA clarity before overweighting.
expert: The +2.78% USD return masks a CAD 5% depreciation (0.77 to 0.73) offsetting a 6.3% local-currency equity gain, implying the total return drag from currency is 340bps; this is unusually high for a developed market and reflects both cyclical capital flight (tariff fears) and structural interest rate differentials (BoC 275bps lower than Fed).

Decomposing the 6.3% TSX gain: cap-weighted indices up 7-8% driven by financials (+8-10%) and energy (+6-8%), while equal-weight indices up 2-3%, suggesting large-cap cyclicals rallied on multiple expansion (not earnings growth) as lower rates boosted valuations; the breadth weakness is a red flag if tariffs materialize.

Forward looking: if tariffs trigger a 3-4% earnings revision downward for Canadian equities while USD strengthens another 2-3% (CAD to 0.70), the USD return could turn negative (-3 to -5%) despite positive local currency performance; watch Q4 2025 earnings for guidance on 2026 margins and capital allocation; if capex guidance drops more than 5%, positioning for CAD underperformance is warranted.

beginner: Canada's economy lost steam in Q2 2025 as exports fell and businesses cut spending, then bounced back in Q3 helped by interest rate cuts. The rebound looks fragile, not structural.

Inflation is way down at 1.78% in February, giving the Bank of Canada room to keep cutting the policy rate (now at 2.25%). That's helping, but it can't fix the real problem: trade uncertainty with the US.

Trump's renegotiation of USMCA could extend tariffs to Chinese goods flowing through Mexico and Canada. That threat hanging over the economy makes businesses hesitant to invest, which is exactly why Q2 was so weak.
moderate: Canada's economy stuttered in Q2 2025 on falling exports and weak business investment, then rebounded in Q3 as the Bank of Canada cut rates to 2.25%. But Q2 weakness with 1.78% inflation shows the economy is fragile, not driven by demand.

The USMCA renegotiation risk is the real headwind. Potential tariffs on Chinese exports transiting Mexico and Canada would force a restructuring of North American supply chains, creating uncertainty that depresses capex even as the central bank loosens.

At 1.78% inflation (well below the 2% target) and policy rates at 2.25%, Canada has room to cut further if growth disappoints. But cutting can't offset tariff shocks, so the BoC is somewhat handcuffed, unlike the Fed facing inflation.
expert: Q2 2025 contraction in exports and investment with Q3 rebound driven by policy easing masks underlying weakness. With CPI at 1.78% and policy rates at 2.25% (versus a 2.25% forecast rate), the BoC is already priced for easing, leaving limited optionality if USMCA tariffs hit.

The Trump administration's signaled extension of China tariffs to Mexican and Canadian re-exports creates a structural supply chain shock. Real capex (business investment) collapsed in Q2 precisely because of this forward-looking uncertainty, and rate cuts cannot offset tariff pass-through.

Watch capex intentions in Q1 2026 data and BoC forward guidance. If tariff uncertainty persists, Canada faces a 1.7% growth forecast requiring demand stimulus, but monetary easing alone cannot overcome trade policy shocks. Fiscal coordination with the US becomes critical.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The Canadian dollar floats freely. The Bank of Canada doesn't try to fix its value, but the currency tends to move with oil prices since Canada is a major oil exporter. CAD/USD shows how many US dollars one Canadian dollar buys. At 0.74, one Canadian dollar buys 74 US cents - or flipped, you give up about 1.35 Canadian dollars to buy one US dollar.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float since 1970. The Bank of Canada has not intervened since 1998. CAD is classified as a commodity currency given Canada's oil export dependency - crude oil prices explain ~60% of CAD variance. The BoC monitors FX as a transmission channel but doesn't target a level.
fxRegime.expert: Free float; last intervention Sept 1998. CAD behaves as a petrocurrency - crude WTI correlation ~0.6 over rolling 12M. Terms of trade channel dominant. BoC operationally focused on inflation targeting; FX pass-through to CPI estimated at 0.05-0.08 over 4Q. Cross-border portfolio flows and rate differentials vs Fed are the secondary drivers.

GDP Growth.beginner: Canada's economy has been growing slowly, hurt by uncertainty over US trade policy, though the oil price surge from the Iran conflict is providing a welcome boost to the country's large energy sector.
GDP Growth.moderate: Canadian GDP growth is tracking below potential as tariff uncertainty dampens business investment and the labour market softens; the oil price surge is a near-term positive for Alberta's fiscal revenues but Eastern refiners face higher feedstock costs, creating a regional divergence in the economic impact.
GDP Growth.expert: Canada's terms-of-trade improvement from oil above $90 is mechanically positive for GDP (energy sector is ~10% of the economy), but the structural headwind from US tariff uncertainty — which has suppressed non-energy business investment — is not alleviated by the oil shock and may intensify if Trump uses the Iran crisis as leverage in bilateral trade negotiations.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Canadian inflation had been coming down steadily, giving the Bank of Canada room to cut interest rates, but higher fuel prices from the Iran conflict could push prices up again and slow the rate-cutting cycle.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Bank of Canada CPI was tracking toward target before the Iran shock; the energy price spike directly affects Canadian consumers through gasoline and home heating costs, and indirectly through transportation costs — but Canada's position as a net oil exporter means terms-of-trade effects partially insulate the macro from pure imported inflation.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Canada's inflation dynamics under the Iran shock are asymmetric by region: Alberta and Saskatchewan (net energy exporters) see income gains that are inflationary from the demand side, while Ontario and Quebec (net energy consumers) face a cost-push inflation impulse; the BoC's national CPI target masks these regional divergences, complicating the optimal monetary policy response.

Unemployment.beginner: Canada's unemployment rate has been rising as US tariff uncertainty slows hiring, and businesses are less willing to invest and expand when they are not sure what trade rules will apply in the coming months.
Unemployment.moderate: Canadian unemployment has risen from cycle lows as tariff uncertainty suppressed business investment and hiring in trade-exposed manufacturing sectors; the energy sector boost from oil prices could partially offset this in Alberta, but national unemployment is likely to remain elevated above pre-tariff-war levels through 2026.
Unemployment.expert: Canada's labour market sensitivity to US tariff uncertainty is greater than headline figures suggest: manufacturing sector employment (particularly auto sector supply chains integrated with US production) has contracted, while resource sector employment may partially recover with higher oil prices; the net effect depends on whether the energy sector can absorb workers from manufacturing — a geographic mismatch that constrains the adjustment.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Canada's government budget is relatively well-managed compared to the US, with a deficit of around 1% of GDP, giving the government more flexibility to use spending to support the economy if needed.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Canada's federal deficit (~1% of GDP) provides significant fiscal space relative to G7 peers; higher oil royalties and corporate taxes from the energy price boom could further improve the fiscal position, giving Ottawa flexibility to deploy targeted energy subsidies or income support without threatening fiscal credibility.
Budget Deficit.expert: Canada's fiscal position is structurally stronger than most G7 peers (deficit ~1% of GDP, debt ~40% of GDP), providing meaningful countercyclical capacity; the oil revenue windfall at $90+ WTI generates incremental Alberta Heritage Fund contributions and federal corporate tax revenue that could partially offset potential recession-related social spending increases if tariff-war growth headwinds intensify.

Current Account.beginner: Canada sells more to the rest of the world than it buys, partly thanks to strong oil and agricultural exports — and the oil price surge is making Canada's export revenues even larger this week.
Current Account.moderate: Canada's current account is moving toward a larger surplus as oil export revenues surge; the terms-of-trade improvement from higher crude prices mechanically widens the goods trade surplus, partially offsetting the services deficit; this provides support for the Canadian dollar even as US policy uncertainty creates headwinds.
Current Account.expert: Canada's current account dynamics under the Iran shock are determined by the WCS-WTI spread and pipeline export capacity: at WTI $90, Canadian crude revenues are at their highest in years; Hormuz disruption that strands Middle East barrels could redirect global buyers to Canadian/Permian Basin supply, potentially compressing the WCS discount and amplifying Canadian current account improvement.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Bank of Canada has been cutting interest rates to support a slowing economy, and with inflation coming under control, more cuts were expected — but higher oil prices could now slow or pause this process.
Policy Rate.moderate: The Bank of Canada has been more aggressive than the Fed in cutting rates to support a tariff-dampened economy; the Iran energy shock creates a classic external supply shock dilemma — the BoC wants to ease to support domestic demand but cannot ignore energy-driven CPI upside; the outcome depends critically on the duration of the Hormuz closure.
Policy Rate.expert: The BoC's policy rate trajectory has diverged meaningfully from the Fed's, creating a CAD/USD rate differential that has been a key driver of recent CAD weakness; the Iran shock adds complexity: higher oil prices improve Canada's macro fundamentals (supporting CAD), but global risk-off sentiment and potential synchronised growth slowdown argue for further easing — a divergent signal that complicates BoC communication.

beginner: The UK economy grew just 1.5% last year, which is barely faster than a country doing nothing, because businesses and households stopped spending after years of inflation pain.
Growth has stuttered twice in two years since Ukraine, meaning the economy keeps stalling instead of building momentum like it should.
At 1.5%, the UK is trapped in slow-growth hell where unemployment stays high and wages struggle to keep pace with living costs.
moderate: The UK expanded 1.5% in 2025 while the US grew roughly 2.5%, showing how much the weak pound and investment drought have held Britain back relative to its peer.
Second consecutive year of stop-start growth reveals structural problems: private investment collapsed and productivity flatlined, not just a cyclical soft patch.
With inflation finally cooling to 2.5% in early 2026, the Bank of England can cut rates further, but 1.5% growth suggests those cuts may arrive too late to revive demand.
expert: Q4 2025 GDP remained weak even as CPI fell 600bps from its peak, indicating demand destruction from prior tightening and real rate shock from 2022-2023 persists.
Private sector investment has collapsed while public capex faces fiscal constraints (4% deficit), leaving 1.5% growth driven entirely by demographic and immigration effects.
Watch Q1 2026 data for any sign that rate cuts and lower energy prices boost consumption; if growth stays sub-2%, the BoE will need to cut 150+bps by year-end.

beginner: Inflation dropped to 2.5%, right at the Bank of England's target, meaning the worst price spike is finally over and your wages might catch up to costs again.
Price growth slowed dramatically in early 2026 after years of double-digit pain, giving households real relief and the central bank room to cut interest rates.
At 2.5%, inflation is no longer the driver of economic misery it was in 2023, but weak growth means the economy may struggle to create enough jobs to feel the benefit.
moderate: CPI fell from double-digit peaks to 2.5% in just 18 months, a faster disinflation than most developed peers, but lagged only because energy shocks hit the UK harder in 2022.
Early 2026 disinflation reflects base effects and weak demand more than wage control; underlying wage growth remains 4-5%, so sticky service inflation could resurface if demand rebounds.
At 2.5%, the BoE has crossed its target and now faces a growth problem, not an inflation problem, shifting policy focus from fighting prices to cutting rates to stimulate output.
expert: CPI hit 2.5% by April 2026 as energy commodity prices stabilized and wage growth finally began to normalize from 5.5% peaks, but core services inflation remains 3.2%.
The disinflation math tilts toward dovish: energy base effects roll off through Q2, but weak demand (1.5% growth) and rising unemployment (5.0%) will suppress price pressures further.
Monitor wage growth and services inflation in May-June data; if both stay above 3.5%, the BoE risks cutting too early and reigniting CPI, forcing a policy reversal by Q3 2026.

beginner: Joblessness hit 5%, meaning 1 in 20 workers is out of work, which is higher than before the pandemic and signals the weak economy is finally hurting the labor market.
After years of tight labor markets, unemployment is rising just as the Bank of England wants to cut rates, creating a bind where job losses could accelerate.
At 5%, there is spare capacity in the job market for the first time since 2021, giving workers less bargaining power and employers less urgency to raise wages.
moderate: Unemployment rose to 5% from 3.8% in mid-2025, a 120bps jump in less than a year, tracking weakness in GDP growth and matching the rise seen in 2020 but without crisis urgency.
The UK jobless rate is now above the eurozone average (3.8%) and closer to US levels (3.9%), showing how the growth stall is finally translating into job losses.
With unemployment trending up and inflation at target, the BoE can cut rates without fear of overheating, but rising joblessness means demand recovery will be slower than policymakers hope.
expert: Unemployment moved from 4.2% (Q3 2025) to 5.0% (Q1 2026) on falling vacancies and weak hiring, driven by tech layoffs and construction pullback, not mass redundancies.
Labor force participation has fallen 40bps since peak, suggesting discouraged workers are exiting the workforce rather than queuing for jobs, masking true slack.
If GDP stays below 2% and business confidence remains depressed (evidenced by 4% deficit), unemployment will drift toward 5.5% by Q4 2026, justifying cumulative rate cuts of 150-175bps.

beginner: The government is borrowing 4% of GDP, which means it spends 4 pounds for every 100 it collects in taxes, a gap the state must fill by selling bonds.
This 4% deficit is high for peacetime and eating into fiscal firepower just as the economy needs help, limiting what policymakers can do to boost growth.
At 4% of GDP, the deficit is unsustainable long-term and means future governments will face pressure to raise taxes or cut spending rather than invest in growth.
moderate: The budget deficit sits at 4% of GDP while growth limps at 1.5%, meaning the state is running big borrowing deficits without the economic growth to justify them or make them manageable.
This 4% gap is double the eurozone average (2%) and reflects both weak tax receipts from slow growth and spending commitments the government locked in years ago.
With the OBR signaling tight fiscal rules and the BoE out of rate ammunition soon, the 4% deficit leaves little room for counter-cyclical policy if growth rolls over into recession in 2026-2027.
expert: The fiscal deficit reached 4.0% of GDP in 2025-26 as tax receipts fell 1.5% YoY despite nominal growth, exposing how weak underlying demand and real wages are destroying the tax base.
Net debt stands at 99% of GDP and trending higher, forcing gilt issuance at 4.43% yields, a level that will cap future fiscal space and eventually crowd out private investment.

If growth stays below 2% and unemployment reaches 5.5%, the structural deficit (adjusted for the cycle) will widen toward 4.5%, triggering calls for austerity that will further suppress demand growth through 2027-28.

beginner: Britain is importing 2.5% more goods and services than it exports, which means the country is borrowing from abroad to cover the shortfall and paying back with future earnings.
This trade deficit reflects weak investment at home and strong spending abroad, draining cash reserves the economy needs to grow and create jobs.
At negative 2.5%, the current account shows the UK is living on borrowed time, relying on foreign buyers of British bonds to fund consumption rather than saving.
moderate: The current account deficit of 2.5% of GDP is narrower than the 4% peaks of 2022 but persistent, driven by goods trade collapse (down 15% since 2021 peak) that post-Brexit investment never replaced.
Manufacturing export volumes remain 8% below pre-pandemic levels while import volumes recovered fully, showing how the trade shock embedded itself into UK supply chains permanently.

A 2.5% deficit is manageable in the short run but unsustainable if it reflects structural loss of export competitiveness rather than cyclical weakness, risking sharp sterling depreciation if foreign investors lose confidence.
expert: The current account deficit of 2.5% of GDP persists even though energy imports have fallen 40% from 2022 peaks, indicating goods trade weakness is fundamental, not energy-driven.
Goods exports fell from 9.2% of GDP (2021) to 7.8% (2025) while the income balance (returns on UK assets abroad) stayed flat at 2.8% of GDP, showing lost manufacturing capacity and low capex returns.

If sterling depreciates below 1.30 per dollar through 2026, import prices will spike and force real demand destruction to close the gap, or the current account deficit will widen toward 3.5%, risking a gilts selloff.

beginner: The Bank of England's base rate stands at 3.25%, which is what the central bank charges banks to borrow overnight and sets the floor for all other interest rates in the economy.
At 3.25%, rates are still elevated to fight inflation, but with prices cooling to 2.5%, the Bank can now start cutting to help the weak economy borrow and spend again.
These rates are expensive for mortgages and loans, choking off growth, so expect the Bank to cut toward 2.5% or lower by year-end to unlock more spending.
moderate: The BoE left rates at 3.25% in March 2026 but signaled cuts are coming as inflation eased to target and growth flatlined, a shift from the tightening cycle that ran from December 2021 through August 2023.
At 3.25%, real rates (3.25% minus 2.5% inflation) are still positive at 0.75%, above the estimated neutral rate of 0.25%, meaning policy remains restrictive and is likely dragging on the 1.5% growth.
Markets now price 125bps of cuts through 2026, implying rates around 2.0% by December, though the BoE may cut slower if unemployment stays high and sterling weakens further.
expert: The BoE held rates at 3.25% on April 3, 2026 but the forward guidance shifted dovish after GDP stalled and CPI hit target, with the next meeting (May 15) viewed as the first cut opportunity.

Real rates of 75bps sit above the estimated r-star of 25-50bps, implying a 25-50bps drag on growth per quarter, and with unemployment at 5.0% and rising, the BoE faces pressure to cut 25bps at each of the next 5 meetings.
Watch May 15 decision for a 25bps cut; if growth rebounds to 2%+ in Q1 data, the BoE may pause, but if unemployment hits 5.5% and gilt yields stay above 4.4%, expect 150bps of cuts by December 2026.

beginner: The stock market is up 6.4% since January 1, 2026, meaning investors are betting that interest rate cuts and lower inflation will help companies earn more profits over time.
This 6.4% gain reflects hope that the Bank of England will cut rates soon, boosting consumer spending and pushing profits higher, even though the real economy is still weak.
If the market continues rallying, it signals that investors believe the worst is over and growth will rebound later in 2026, but that remains a bet, not yet a reality.
moderate: The FTSE 100 returned 6.4% YTD through April 2026, outperforming a stalled economy by pricing in rate cuts worth roughly 125bps and a re-rating of cyclical stocks on recovery hopes.

This gain trails the US market (roughly 10% YTD in pounds), reflecting the UK's smaller weighting to mega-cap tech and higher exposure to commodities and financials, which benefit less from disinflation.

The 6.4% rally assumes the BoE cuts rates aggressively and growth rebounds to 2%+ by mid-2026, but with unemployment rising and investment collapsed, the upside is capped unless external demand (US or EU) suddenly strengthens.
expert: The FTSE 100 gained 6.4% YTD as sterling weakness (GBP/USD fell from 1.28 to 1.35) boosted foreign currency earnings and rate-cut expectations pushed equity risk premiums lower by roughly 60bps.

Cyclical stock performance (banks, miners) improved 12-15% while defensives (utilities, consumer staples) gained only 2-4%, indicating the market is pricing a V-shaped recovery scenario that contradicts the 1.5% growth backdrop.

If Q1 GDP data (released April 25) shows a rebound to 0.6%+ quarterly growth, the market could push higher toward 7.5% gains, but if it confirms flat growth and unemployment pushes toward 5.2%, expect a 3-5% pullback by June.

beginner: The 10-year bond yield is 4.43%, which is what the government pays to borrow money for a decade, and this high rate reflects inflation worries and fiscal deficits that investors are still wary of.
At 4.43%, borrowing costs are expensive for the government and for businesses, meaning less investment and less growth, creating a vicious cycle.

Watch this yield for any signs it falls below 4%; if it does, it means investors see a recession coming and are fleeing to safety, which would hurt stocks and confirm the economic slowdown is worsening.
moderate: The 10Y gilt yield stands at 4.43%, which is 75bps above the policy rate of 3.25%, a spread that reflects term premiums and inflation uncertainty, not fiscal distress (the US 10Y sits at roughly 4.5%).

This 4.43% level is above the estimated nominal potential growth rate (2.5%), meaning gilt investors are demanding a premium for owning UK debt in a low-growth environment with sticky fiscal deficits.
If the BoE cuts rates as expected (125bps by December), the 10Y should fall toward 3.8-4.0%, assuming the yield curve normalizes and inflation expectations remain anchored below 2.5%.
expert: The 10Y yield of 4.43% reflects a 220bps real yield (4.43% minus 2.23% breakeven inflation rate) that is pricing in structural fiscal deficits and weak growth, not a recession premium like 2020.

Term premiums in gilts sit roughly 50bps wide of Bunds and 70bps tight to Treasuries, suggesting the market is pricing UK policy rates 125-150bps lower than the US by year-end, a bet on more aggressive BoE cuts.
If unemployment reaches 5.5% by August and Q2 GDP remains flat, expect 10Y yields to fall toward 3.9% by October as the market prices a BoE funds rate of 2.0% or lower by December, a 125bps move.

beginner: The yield curve is at plus 72 basis points, which measures how much extra return you get for lending money for 10 years instead of overnight, and higher numbers mean the economy looks stable.
At 72bps, the curve is positive, meaning investors trust the long-term outlook more than they fear a near-term recession, so lending and investment should continue.
Watch for the curve to flatten below 50bps; if it does, investors are getting scared about the economy and may start pulling back from lending, which would slow growth even further.
moderate: The curve is 72bps steep (10Y gilt minus overnight rate), which is normal for a weak growth period but narrower than historical averages of 100-120bps, signaling investor caution.
This 72bps slope compares to the US curve at roughly 25bps, showing UK investors are more optimistic about future rate cuts (which steepen curves) than US peers, a bet on aggressive BoE easing.
If the BoE cuts rates 125bps as markets expect and the 10Y stays flat, the curve will flatten toward 40-50bps by Q4 2026, a level that would suggest recession risk is rising.
expert: The 10Y-OIS spread of 72bps reflects expectations of 125-150bps of rate cuts through December 2026, with the curve pricing terminal rates of 2.0-2.25% versus the current 3.25%.
Historical correlations suggest a 72bps UK curve (versus 25bps US curve) implies the market is pricing synchronized recession risk in 2027, forcing parallel rate cuts, but with a 6-month UK lag.

If the May 15 BoE decision delivers a 25bps cut and Q2 GDP data (released in August) shows a rebound to 0.4%+ quarterly, the curve will steepen toward 85-90bps as market pricing for terminal rates shifts higher to 2.5%.

beginner: The pound is trading at 1.35 per dollar, which means one pound buys fewer dollars than it used to, so British exports are cheaper for foreigners but imports are more expensive at home.
A weak pound (down from 1.40 a year ago) reflects weak UK growth and investor worries that the economy will underperform, pushing capital out and weakening the currency.
If the pound continues falling below 1.30, imports will become very expensive, inflation could spike, and the Bank of England may have to keep rates higher for longer, choking growth further.
moderate: GBP/USD has slipped from 1.40 (mid-2025) to 1.35 (April 2026), a 3.6% depreciation driven by rate differentials (BoE cuts expected versus US rates staying higher) and growth differentials (US at 2.5% versus UK at 1.5%).
The weak pound supports exporters in nominal terms but does nothing to solve the real problem: low capex and lost market share mean UK export volumes are structurally depressed, not cyclically weak.

At 1.35, the pound is near fair value for the growth differential, but further weakness to 1.25-1.30 would trigger imported inflation and force the BoE to cut less than markets now expect, a negative feedback loop.
expert: GBP/USD fell from 1.40 to 1.35 as the 10Y real yield fell 50bps relative to the US, with the UK 2.23% breakeven inflation rate 15bps below the US level, indicating expectations of UK disinflation exceeding the US.

Net positioning from real money investors (pensions, insurance) has shifted from long GBP (late 2023) to neutral (early 2026) as the growth consensus shifted from UK stabilization to fiscal/demographic stagnation.
If the BoE delivers 150bps of cuts by December and the Fed cuts only 75bps, GBP/USD could fall to 1.28-1.32 by year-end, pushing import prices up 3-5% and forcing a partial policy reversal in 2027.

beginner: When you convert the 6.4% UK stock gain into dollars using today's exchange rate, you get only 5.25%, because the pound weakened and that eats into the return for US investors.
The gap between 6.4% in pounds and 5.25% in dollars (about 1.15 percentage points) shows that currency weakness is costing American investors real money, even when UK stocks are rising.
This means US investors in British stocks are losing to the S&P 500 (which is up roughly 10% in dollars) not because UK companies are bad, but because the pound is falling.
moderate: FTSE 100 returned 6.4% in GBP but only 5.25% in USD through April 2026, a currency drag of 115bps that reflects the 3.6% GBP/USD depreciation from 1.40 to 1.35.
This currency headwind is real for US investors and explains why UK equity allocations have been cut by global funds; capital depreciation on sterling holdings is washing away equity gains.
If GBP/USD falls further to 1.30 by year-end, the currency drag could reach 200bps, meaning a 6.4% GBP return would net only 4.4% in USD terms, a reason many US investors are underweight UK equities.
expert: The 115bps currency drag (6.4% GBP return minus 5.25% USD return) maps to a 3.6% sterling depreciation year-to-date, with the pound falling from 1.403 (January 1) to 1.349 (April 14) on growth and rate expectations.

Realized volatility of GBP/USD has remained elevated at 11-12%, creating a -65bps drag from negative gamma for long equity / long GBP positions, meaning the combination underperforms equity-only longs.

If BoE cuts accelerate to 150-175bps by December while the Fed cuts only 75bps, GBP/USD could reach 1.28 by year-end, compounding to a 220bps+ currency drag and bringing USD-adjusted returns down to 4% or lower despite positive local performance.

beginner: The UK economy has been flatlining for two years straight, stumbling after Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted trade and energy. That's an unusually long period of stagnation for a major economy.
